Rules / Performance

SK4030 The collection's own method answers this faster than the LINQ extension

List<T> and ImmutableList<T> declare Find, Exists and TrueForAll; the Enumerable extension that answers the same question allocates an enumerator to do it.

CategoryPerformance
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, review it
Language version floor—
Since1.3
SupersedesS6602, S6603, S6605, S6617

Why

FirstOrDefault, Any and All are written against IEnumerable<T>, so they allocate an enumerator, drive it through MoveNext and call the predicate through it. Find, Exists and TrueForAll are members of the list, so they walk the backing array with an index and allocate nothing. The delegate is the same object under two names — Predicate<T> and Func<T, bool> have identical signatures — so the substitution costs the reader nothing either. Any(x => x == v) is a third case of the same argument and the sharpest: Contains(v) needs no delegate at all, and the comparison ends up somewhere the reader can see it.

Example

Instead of:

var ready = items.FirstOrDefault(item => item.IsReady);
var anyReady = items.Any(item => item.IsReady);
var known = names.Any(name => name == wanted);

Write:

var ready = items.Find(item => item.IsReady);
var anyReady = items.Exists(item => item.IsReady);
var known = names.Contains(wanted);

When it does not fire

⚠ Every pair was checked on the empty sequence, which is where a substitution like this goes wrong, and none of them changes a return. All is vacuously true and TrueForAll returns true over zero elements; Any and Exists are both false; FirstOrDefault and Find both return default(T) — for a value type as well, so neither throws where the other does not. First, Single and SingleOrDefault are deliberately outside the table, because Find returns a default where those throw. ⚠ The receiver must be `List<T>` or `ImmutableList<T>` as the semantic model resolves it, never a type that merely has a member of the right name. A set carries an IEqualityComparer<T>, so HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase).Contains(v) and Any(x => x == v) genuinely disagree, and that is the false positive this restriction exists to prevent. ⚠ The Any(x => x == v) rewrite additionally requires an element type whose default equality comparer is its ==: string, the integral types, char, bool, decimal and any enum. double and float are excluded because NaN == NaN is false where EqualityComparer<double>.Default.Equals(NaN, NaN) is true and -0.0 == 0.0 is true where Equals is false; reference types are excluded because == may be identity, or an operator somebody wrote. The compared value must also be a name path or a literal. ⚠ The predicate must be written as a lambda or an anonymous method. A Func<T, bool> variable does not convert to Predicate<T> — the fix would be CS1503 — and a method group is left alone as the cheaper miss. ⚠ A predicate that mutates the list is not guarded, and building a guard for it would mean proving a lambda pure. ⚠ The reason this sentence used to give was measured false on .NET 10: Any, All and FirstOrDefault over a List<T> iterate a span taken once rather than a version-checked enumerator, so nothing throws — what differs is that Find and TrueForAll read the live size (#430). ⚠ #423: the compared value must be free to skip — it runs no code and cannot throw — because Contains(v) evaluates it once where the lambda evaluated it once per element, and never on an empty list. Any(x => x == cursor.Next) over a counting getter, and Any(x => x == holder.Value) with a null holder, are no longer rewritten to Contains; they fall through to Exists, which keeps the lambda. ⚠ The fix is still not safe, for a reason outside #423: Find and TrueForAll read the list's live _size where Enumerable snapshots through its enumerator, so a predicate that adds or removes elements sees a different sequence — All → TrueForAll measured False → True (#430).
